                                          ARGUMENT



   I.       ELL Lacks Standing to Object to the   Issuance of the Subpoena

   The Commission clearly has the power to subpoena documents and other materials relevant


to issues under its jurisdiction. The Louisiana Supreme Court has ruled that the &RPPLVVLRQ¶V



powers to issue a subpoena are the same as those of the Louisiana district courts. Standard Oil


Company 0fL0uisiana v. Louisiana Pub. Serv. Comm ¶Q 154 La. 557, 570, 97 So. 859, 864
 (1923). Thus, the principles which apply to Louisiana FRXUWV¶ subpoena power also apply to the

&RPPLVVLRQ¶V subpoena power.



   The applicable Louisiana rule in this instance is La.C.C.P. art. 1354. The Louisiana courts


have held that this rule only contemplates motions to quash be ¿OHG by the party on whom the


subpoena is served. Arnaud v. Scottsdale Ins. Co., 14-1809 at p. 13, 182 So.3d 97, 105 (La.App.

1 Cir. 2015). Under both Louisiana and federal law, only the person or entity served with a


subpoena has the legal right to object, unless another party can demonstrate a personal right or

privilege in the information requested. See, e.g., US. v. Gordon, 247 F.R.D. 509, 509 (E.D. N.C.

2007). See, also, Kiger v. Plaisance Dragline, Civ. A. 04-3453, 2006 WL 3228289, at *1 (E.D.

La. Nov. 2, 2006) (Roby, J.) Importantly, the claim of privilege or right must be personal to the


objecting party, not to the nonparty witness on whom the subpoena was served. Samad Bros.,

Inc. v. Bokara Rug Co. Inc., 2010 WL 5094344 at *2 (S.D.N.Y. 2010).



    The recipient of a VXESRHQD²²WKH individual or organization to be directly VHUYHG²LV the


party with standing to object. This is because the subpoena imposes a legal obligation only on

the recipient of the subpoena to produce documents and they bear the potential consequences of


noncompliance.


   Louisiana discovery rules are also based upon the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and the


Louisiana courts look to that source to as an aid to interpreting the Louisiana rules. Collins v.


Crosby Group, Inc., 551 So.2d 42, 43 (La App. l Cir. 1989), writs denied, 556 So.2d 39, 42 (La.

1990). See, also, State v. Louisiana Land & Exploration Co., 18-0890 at p. 6, 272 So.3d 937, 942

(La.App. 3 Cir. 2019). The Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45 ³5XOH ´        governs federal


subpoena practice.

                                            CONCLUSION



    It is a basic principle of law that a tribunal cannot act on a SDUW\¶V motion where that party


lacks standing. Under both Louisiana and federal law, only the person or entity served with a


subpoena has the legal right to object, unless another party can demonstrate a personal right or

privilege in the information requested. Importantly, the claim of privilege or right must be

personal to the objecting party, not to the nonparty witness on whom the subpoena was served.
